description: How speech is LEARNED — the sensorimotor babble feedback loop at the centre, plus the perceptual narrowing + statistical learning that build the native sound system.

sub_mechanisms.name: vocal_play_cooing
sub_mechanisms.definition: Early non-speech phonation (cooing, vocal play; ~2-4 months) that exercises phonation + the vocal apparatus and begins linking motor acts to heard sound.
sub_mechanisms.why: The pre-canonical groundwork: the infant discovers it can make sound and hear it, seeding the perception-production link.

sub_mechanisms.name: canonical_babbling
sub_mechanisms.definition: Rhythmic, well-timed, reduplicated consonant-vowel syllables (baba, dada; ~6-10 months) — the first speech-like, adult-timed production.
sub_mechanisms.why: The behavioural onset of speech production; its emergence is a developmental milestone and the substrate of the feedback loop.

sub_mechanisms.name: babble_feedback_loop
sub_mechanisms.definition: THE core sensorimotor loop: the infant PRODUCES a sound, HEARS its own output, compares the heard result to the intended/target acoustics, and uses the MISMATCH to tune the articulation -> acoustics -> perception mapping. Self-generated, self-supervised, runs thousands of times.
sub_mechanisms.why: This is how the perception-production map is grounded WITHOUT a labelled teacher — the mismatch signal is the training signal. It is the agent's own babble loop, and the reason babies babble.

sub_mechanisms.name: perception_production_link
sub_mechanisms.definition: Hearing one's own babble grounds a bidirectional map between motor commands and acoustic/perceptual targets, so the infant can later IMITATE heard speech (reproduce an external target with its own articulators).
sub_mechanisms.why: Imitation + vocal learning require an inverse model (target sound -> motor command); the babble loop builds it.

sub_mechanisms.name: perceptual_narrowing
sub_mechanisms.definition: Infants begin as UNIVERSAL listeners (discriminate the contrasts of all languages) and NARROW to native contrasts by ~10-12 months, losing sensitivity to non-native distinctions; the perceptual feature space shrinks to what the ambient language uses.
sub_mechanisms.why: Experience prunes the category space to the native inventory — efficiency at the cost of universal discrimination; a clear use-it-or-lose-it learning signature.

sub_mechanisms.name: statistical_learning
sub_mechanisms.definition: Infants track distributional + transitional-probability regularities in the input — co-occurrence statistics across syllables to find word boundaries, and the distribution of cue values to find category structure.
sub_mechanisms.why: Much of the sound system + early segmentation is learned by tracking statistics of unlabelled input, not by explicit instruction.

sub_mechanisms.name: distributional_learning_of_categories
sub_mechanisms.definition: The SHAPE of the input distribution along a phonetic cue determines categories: a bimodal distribution along VOT yields two categories, a unimodal one yields one. Infants form categories to fit the modes of what they hear.
sub_mechanisms.why: Explains WHY native categories end up where they do — they are carved at the valleys between modes in the ambient distribution.

sub_mechanisms.name: categorical_perception_formation
sub_mechanisms.definition: Over development, continuous acoustic dimensions get carved into native categories: identification boundaries sharpen and within-category discrimination drops as the categories consolidate (~6-12 months for many contrasts).
sub_mechanisms.why: The developmental ORIGIN of adult categorical perception; it is learned, not innate, and tracks the ambient language.

sub_mechanisms.name: variegated_babbling
sub_mechanisms.definition: Babbling with varied consonants + vowels and adult-like intonation contours (~10-12 months), increasingly resembling the ambient language; the bridge to first words.
sub_mechanisms.why: Production becoming language-specific; the motor system is now exploring the native inventory, not just reduplicated syllables.

sub_mechanisms.name: ambient_language_tuning
sub_mechanisms.definition: Both perception and production drift toward the ambient language: babbling takes on native sounds + prosody, and perception tunes to native categories. The child becomes a native speaker-hearer.
sub_mechanisms.why: The convergence point of the loop — input shapes output, output (heard back) shapes the map; the system specialises to one language.

sub_mechanisms.name: vocabulary_explosion
sub_mechanisms.definition: Once phonological categories stabilise (~18 months), the rate of word learning jumps sharply (from ~0.1 to several words/day) — a phase change, not a smooth ramp.
sub_mechanisms.why: Stable sound categories make word-forms reliably distinguishable, unlocking fast lexical acquisition; the payoff of the whole loop.

derivation_rules.name: acquisition_babble_is_self_supervised
then: the produce->hear MISMATCH grounds the perception-production map
derivation_rules.why: The loop trains itself; the error signal is the difference between intended and self-heard output. This is why babies babble.

derivation_rules.name: acquisition_distribution_sets_categories
then: native categories carved at the distribution's valleys
derivation_rules.why: Categories are learned to fit the modes of unlabelled input; the boundary sits where the input is sparse.

derivation_rules.name: acquisition_narrowing_then_explosion
derivation_rules.why: Stable, native, well-separated categories are the precondition for fast word learning; the milestones are causally ordered.
